S03.basis: With its shafts open a King's Chamber of pure sulfur dioxide loses half its charge by diffusion in 361 (271 to 460) years, and no wind below 29 (23 to 43) m/s can drive a through-flow, because the gas, 2.2 times as dense as air, would have to be lifted up the leeward shaft against 516 (472 to 551) Pa. The same weight carries it out of an opening at the chamber's floor while no water stands beyond it and the Gallery is open to the air, which the hypothesis does not say for the time before the fill: through the 202 cm2 of grooves and one slab's clearance in the antechamber, the gas path of the hypothesis, half the charge is gone in about 69 minutes (41 at the fastest, never with the path shut). In the 30 m/s at the top of the assumed wind range the half-time falls to 15 minutes, and to 11 with the floor opening draining at its fastest as well, against the interval between delivery and draw, which the hypothesis does not state and which is taken as 10 minutes to 30 days; a charge diluted to a tenth is held only below 9 m/s, and below the wind that lifts it the model loses gas up the shafts by diffusion alone, which is a limit of the model. Remaining is read as half the charge still being there at the draw, and the hypothesis states neither the composition of the charge nor what keeps it in.

S08.basis: The highest water documented at Khufu or beside it, the Old Kingdom flood peak or today's water table, stands 15 (10 to 18) m below the foot of the Descending Passage; the chamber's deepest floor lies 1.9 m and the pit's original bottom up to 5.1 m lower than that foot, still above that water. Perched water at 22 to 48 m above sea level is interpreted from geophysics toward Menkaure and none is reported at Khufu, so it is not counted. No documented water therefore reaches the Subterranean Chamber, and the step holds only for a reservoir that is assumed: the hypothesis names one without level, volume or inlet, and nothing on site attests it. It must stand at pavement level or above and enter by a conduit that no survey shows, or 17.0 m above the pavement to use the entrance, the only surveyed opening; to fill the Gallery by communicating vessels alone it must stand 51.5 m above the pavement, 112 (109 to 114) m above sea level. One fill takes 866 (808 to 924) m3, an inflow of 0.24 m3/s if it takes 1 h, after 385 (284 to 536) m3 to prime the Subterranean Chamber and the Descending Passage up to the pavement.

S13.basis: With the Gallery full to its roof the water stands 8.5 (8.3 to 8.6) m above the antechamber floor and presses with 83 kPa, so an opening that passes gas passes water: past slabs as loose as the surviving fragment 0.16 (0.14 to 0.26) m3/s enter and the water stands at the King's Chamber shaft mouths after 6 (4 to 7) minutes, through the 20 cm2 of the grooves alone after 1.0 h, and with the path shut no gas passes either. Holding the water back would take 83 kPa of gas pressure, which the open shafts release in 53 s, and with the shafts shut the water still rises 2.2 m or more in the chamber. Water stays out only if the fill stops at the antechamber floor, 43.0 m above the pavement, and the hypothesis states no drain route.

S14.basis: The antechamber opening lies 7.4 m under the surface of the full Gallery, and until 13.2 (12.7 to 13.3) percent of the Gallery has drained gas enters it only where the suction exceeds the water standing over it, 72 kPa at the start. Draining the Gallery in 1 h through 202 cm2 of grooves and one slab's clearance, with masonry joints of 0.51 mm leaking along a path of 1.0 m, 60 percent of the replacement gas comes down the King's Chamber shafts; the pressure difference is 195 Pa at the start, when the joints alone supply the pocket, and 60 Pa once the opening is clear. Over drain times of 10 minutes to 6 h, joints of 0.05 to 0.51 mm and joint paths of 0.3 to 3.0 m the share runs from 20 to 100 percent with that path open, and from 0 percent if the path is shut, as blind grooves and seated slabs would leave it; the pressure difference runs from 1 Pa to 99 kPa, the most a water column can pull. Through the grooves alone the share is 11 percent, through the three slabs' clearances one after another, which pass what 108 cm2 passes, 44 percent, and with no slab in the passage 78 percent. More than half comes down the shafts with the joints tighter than 0.64 mm, or the drain slower than 30 minutes; the hypothesis states neither a drain rate nor how the Gallery is made gas-tight.

S17.basis: Of the Gallery's five surveyed openings the Ascending Passage, the Queen's passage and the well shaft meet it at its foot and stay under water until 0.7 percent of it or less is left, and Davison's passage ends in a closed chamber. The antechamber opening lies 7.4 m under the surface of the full Gallery, and until 13.2 (12.7 to 13.3) percent of the Gallery has drained gas enters it only where the suction exceeds the water standing over it, 72 kPa at the start. With gas-tight masonry nothing else can enter, so 100.0 (99.9 to 100.0) percent of the displaced volume is drawn through the antechamber passage as surveyed, with no slab in it. Counting gas that leaks in through 1350 m of masonry joints of 0.05 to 0.51 mm, from air-filled masonry at outside pressure 0.3 to 3.0 m behind the Gallery's face, a leak that is assumed and that 01 leaves open for the syringe, the share is 78 (38 to 100) percent over drain times of 10 minutes to 6 h and passes 90 percent with joints tighter than 0.11 (0.04 to 0.24) mm or somewhat wider, the model letting neither the pocket's gas thin nor Davison's chamber lend. With the slabs of the hypothesis down the two shares are 100.0 and 60 percent through 202 cm2 of grooves and one slab's clearance, and nothing if that path is shut, which is the question of S15.
